questions.q: What layer does Infrastructure as Code (IaC) cover, distinct from Lessons 45-46's CI/CD and Git integration?
options: The actual Azure resources a Fabric workspace depends on, like the Event Hub namespace and the Fabric Capacity itself
The same Fabric item definitions already covered by Git integration
Only Power BI report formatting
Only KQL query syntax
questions.explain: Those Azure resources are provisioned through Azure, not through Fabric's own Git integration, and need their own definition.

questions.q: What does a Bicep template describe?
options: The desired end state — "this resource should exist, with this configuration" — rather than a sequence of manual steps
A sequence of manual click-by-click portal instructions
Only KQL query logic
A CI/CD pipeline's test stage
questions.explain: Running it against an environment that already matches the definition does nothing; running it against an empty one creates everything described.

questions.q: What is Terraform's key difference from Bicep, despite expressing the same declarative idea?
options: Terraform works across multiple clouds (AWS, GCP, etc.) via a provider model, while Bicep is Azure-only
Terraform can only be used for Fabric items, never Azure resources
Bicep is cloud-agnostic while Terraform is Azure-only
There's no real difference between the two tools at all
questions.explain: This makes Terraform useful for a team managing infrastructure across more than one cloud.

questions.q: Why does manually clicking through the Azure portal have the same problem as Lesson 45's manual "click Deploy" issue?
options: It can't guarantee dev, test, and prod end up configured identically, and there's no record of exactly what was clicked
The Azure portal doesn't actually allow creating resources manually
Manual portal clicks are always faster and more reliable than IaC
This problem only applies to Fabric items, never to underlying Azure resources
questions.explain: IaC solves it the same way CI/CD solved deployment — a definition file replaces institutional memory.

questions.q: What happens when a Bicep or Terraform definition is run against an environment that already matches it?
options: Nothing — the declarative definition only creates or changes what's actually different from the desired end state
It always recreates every resource from scratch, causing downtime
It throws an error and refuses to run
It deletes the existing resources first
questions.explain: This is the core benefit of declarative infrastructure — the same file can be safely run repeatedly.
